analytic.title: Enhanced Virtual Release Advancing for EDF-based Scheduling on Precise Real-Time Systems

div.p: In precise real-time systems, scheduling algorithms without considerable complexity are more effective to be applied. Virtual release advancing [3] for shorter response times is a technique that is valuable for the Earliest Deadline First (EDF) scheduling, but not adaptive to precise systems due to its high time complexity. A new scheduling algorithm, called enhanced virtual release advancing, that mitigates the time complexity, is presented in this paper. Applied in the Total Bandwidth Server (TBS) context, the new algorithm significantly improves the time complexity while guaranteeing the responsiveness and schedulability. Simulation results show that the runtime overhead is approximately 56% lower than that of the original algorithm under the periodic processor utilization of 95%.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: In real-time systems, together with deadline requirements, response time is an important factor to task scheduling's effectiveness. Improving response time for aperiodic tasks becomes the goal of techniques: the adaptive total bandwidth server (Adaptive TBS) [1], the adaptive EDF [2], and the virtual release advancing [3]. These techniques have been trying to assign the target aperiodic task an earlier deadline that may lead to an earlier scheduling based on the EDF algorithm [4] in the Total Bandwidth Server (TBS) context [5]. In order to obtain an earlier deadline, the virtual release advancing technique introduces a virtual release time earlier than task's actual release time in the deadline calculation. This technique shows its remarkable improvement in terms of task's responsiveness. However, its time complexity is relatively high. The runtime overhead of the technique reaches around 0.9% of the tick length of 1 millisecond as shown in Figure 4 in the literature [3]. The high time complexity can prevent the technique from being applied to precise real-time systems the tick of which may be less than 0.1 milisecond in length.

To alleviate the time complexity of the virtual release advancing technique, an enhanced virtual release advancing (EVRA) algorithm is proposed. This algorithm introduces boundary deadlines as limits of advancing and then tries to satisfy these limits to obtain suitable virtual deadlines. Especially, the enhanced points of the algorithm are techniques to reduce the loop count that mainly causes the runtime overhead in the original algorithm. The contribution of the new algorithm is that the time complexity is reduced while the schedulability and responsiveness are still guaranteed.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: The study is to mitigate the time complexity of the virtual release advancing technique. The basics of the virtual release advancing technique are hence described in this section.

Virtual release advancing (VRA) is a technique based on the TBS server [5] and the EDF algorithm. This technique is aimed to introduce an earlier deadline by virtually and retroactively moving a release time backward to the past while maintaining the past schedule. Equation 1 is the original TBS formula. In this equation, k means k-th aperiodic task, d k is the absolute deadline of the k-th aperiodic task, r k is release (arrival) time of the k-th aperiodic task, d k-1 is the absolute deadline of the k-1-th (previous) task, C k is worst-case execution time of the k-th task, and U s is the bandwidth of the server.
div.formula: d k = max(r k , d k-1 ) + C k U s(1)
div.p: The earlier deadline then may lead to an earlier scheduling for the target task under the EDF algorithm. Figure 1 shows an example of the technique with two periodic tasks. The first periodic task, τ 1 , has a period T 1 = 3 and an execution time C 1 = 1. Similarly, the second periodic task, τ 2 , has T 2 = 6 and C 2 = 3. The processor utilization by the periodic tasks is U p = 1/3 + 1/2 = 5/6 and then the bandwidth of the TBS server is U s = 1 -5/6 = 1/6. It is assumed that there is an aperiodic task entering the system at t = 8 with its execution time of 1. According to the original TBS scheduling, the aperiodic task has deadline of t = 14, finishing time at t = 12, and response time of 4.

In this case, by applying the virtual release advancing technique, a virtual release time for the aperiodic task is set up at t = 6 as indicated by a red, upward dashed arrow. According to this new release time, the deadline calculation in TBS would give a deadline at t = 12 , two ticks earlier than the original deadline. This new deadline, as depicted by a red, downward dashed arrow, is the same as that of the fourth instance of τ 1 . Since the aperiodic tasks are more preemptive than periodic tasks, the target aperiodic task is executed ahead of the periodic instance and finishes sooner at t = 11 with the response time of 3.

The virtual release advancing technique tries to obtain an earlier virtual release time for the target aperiodic task based on three factors: previous aperiodic task's deadline, last empty slot, and maximum previously-used deadline [3]. These factors are known as the limits of how long the release time can be advanced. It is stated that moving release time backward over any one of these limits is ineffective or leads to changing the past schedules.

For the first limit, since this technique follows the Equation 1, the TBS server always chooses the larger one between the previous aperiodic task's deadline and the target task's release time when calculating the absolute deadline. Moving release time backward over this limit has no effects.

Next limit is the last empty slot. An empty slot is defined as the time slot without task's execution. In the example in Figure 1, slot 5 is an empty slot. If the release time is advanced over an empty slot, the slot should be spent by the task. It is understood that the past schedule is changed. Therefore, the advancing in this case is not eligible.

The final limit is the maximum previously-used deadline. Used slots are time slots with an task's associated deadline that is assigned to the slots. If task's virtual deadline calculated with the advanced release time is earlier than the associated deadline of the slot, the slot must be spent for the task. This means the past schedule is changed. The advanced release time in this case is not allowable.

Although it shows effectiveness in improving the response time of target tasks, the virtual release advancing technique has a problem with its high runtime overhead. Due to the high runtime overhead, the algorithm has just been evaluated on systems with a relatively long tick length of 1 millisecond. In order to apply to more precise systems, an algorithm with light-weight complexity is required.

div.head: III. ENHANCED VIRTUAL RELEASE ADVANCING A. Causes of overhead in the original algorithm
div.p: As mentioned above, the goal of virtual release advancing is to obtain as earlier virtual release time as possible than the actual one. To achieve this goal, the technique checks limit factors slot by slot from the target task's arrival time (r k ) backward to the past. Checking stops and the virtual release time as well as the virtual deadline is obtained when one of factors is reached. A whole while loop [3] is implemented for the checking.

The algorithm increases runtime overhead as follows. Firstly, the algorithm checks two factors, previous deadline and last empty slot, in every iteration. However, there are actually only one previous deadline and one last empty slot. Thus, it is desirable to check only once for each factor. Secondly, consecutive slots spent by the same instance of tasks are checked one by one. It is obviously unnecessary since these slots have the same associated deadline. Once again, it is desirable to check only the representative one of slots.
The EVRA technique is eligible to overcome these difficulties.

div.head: B. Definitions of EVRA
div.p: In order to clearly present the proposed technique, it is necessary to explain first the following definitions: boundary deadlines, check-bounding slot, and representative slots.

1) Boundary deadlines: As mentioned in the previous section, in the original VRA algorithm there are three limits of advancing: the previous aperiodic task's deadline, the last empty slot, and the maximum previously-used deadline. The first two limits are directly compared to a tentative virtual release time in each loop iteration. It is different from the proposed algorithm where these two factors are converted to the corresponding deadlines to be dealt with outside of the loop. For example in Figure 2, let us consider the second aperiodic task arriving at t = 9 with C k2 = 1. The previous aperiodic task's deadline is at t = 7 and the last empty slot is slot 7. Using the previous deadline (t = 7) and the tick time (t = 8) just after the empty slot as replacements for r k in Equation 1, two corresponding deadlines (vd k2 and vd k2 ) for the target task are calculated to be at t = 13 and t = 14, respectively.

div.head: Fig. 2. Example of boundary deadlines
div.p: These two deadlines are considered as two boundary deadlines of the proposed algorithm. Another boundary deadline is related to the calculation of the check-bounding slot which is coming in the next subsection. In order to satisfy the limits of the algorithm, the expected virtual deadline for the target task hence has to be greater than or equal to all of these boundary deadlines.

2) Check-bounding slot: Given τ max is the periodic task having the maximum period T max , and ls max is the starting time of the last instance of τ max . Under the EDF algorithm, the associated deadline of ls max -th slot is greater than or equal to the associated deadline of slots before it. That is, we have:

where dl[x] and dl[ls max ] are the associated deadlines of the x -th slot and the ls max -th slot, respectively. Figure 3 shows an illustration for the check-bounding slot. In this example, τ 2 corresponds to τ max . Let us assume that the current aperiodic task's release time is at 7, then the last instance of τ max is the instance executed from slot 1 to slot 4. Therefore, ls max is identified at t = 1. Note that the maximum previously-used deadline has to be determined at each iteration of the virtual release advancing. Since the ls max -th slot has the greater associated deadline than that of previous slots according to Equation 2, looking for the maximum previouslyused deadline on slots before the ls max -th slot is obviously unnecessary. Therefore, when advancing under the limit of the maximum previously-used deadline, slots from r k backward to ls max should be scanned ones only. ls max is beneficially chosen as the check-bounding slot and this slot's associated deadline is considered as the third boundary deadline of the proposed algorithm. 3) Representative slots of instances: As discussed above, checking all of slots of the same instance one by one is unnecessary. Instead, the first slot of each instance is chosen as the representative. In Figure 4, for instance, slot 0 and slot 1 are considered as representative slots for τ 1 and τ 2 , respectively.

For this example, the original VRA algorithm checks all slots from t = 4 backward to t = 0, that is, slot 3, 2, 1, and 0. However, the enhanced algorithm checks slot 0 and 1 only for the advancing. It is obviously more effective in terms of the check loop count and memory use.

div.head: C. Processing flow of the EVRA algorithm
div.p: For making an overview of the EVRA algorithm, the processing flow is shown in Figure 5. In the processing flow, there are three checking conditions denoted as L1, L2, and L3, respectively. L1 is the previous tasks deadline; L2 is the boundary deadlines; and L3 is the maximum previously-used deadlines. The proposed algorithm starts with creating and initiating variables. Then the limit of the previous aperiodic task's deadline (represented by L1) is expected to be calculated and checked first outside of the advancing loop. If the release time is equal to or less than the previous aperiodic task's deadline, the scheduling process stops. Otherwise, the process continues to calculate the boundary deadlines.

After calculating the boundary deadlines, a loop of virtual deadline advancing (denoted by the part in orange) begins under the condition of the boundary deadlines (considered as L2). In the advancing loop, the maximum previously-used deadline is updated first and then compared to the current virtual deadline (considered as condition L3). In the case that L3 is not satisfied, the loop breaks and then the advancing process stops. If L3 is passed, the virtual deadline is advanced backward to the past by one instance. Continously, L3 is checked again and if it is passed, the loop is repeated for the next advancing.

The virtual deadline advancing loop is repeated until one of L2 or L3 is broken; it means a stop state is generated. It is important to note that in the proposed algorithm the eventual virtual deadline is obviously updated with alternative values depending on which condition leads to the stop state. These values are made clear in the detailed algorithm in the next subsection.

div.head: D. Algorithm for EVRA
div.p: The whole EVRA algorithm is shown in Algorithm 1. In the algorithm, r k and vr k are the real and virtual release times of the target aperiodic task, respectively. vd k is the expected virtual deadline. C k and U s are tasks execution time and the bandwidth of TBS server. d k-1 is the deadline of the k-1-th (previous) aperiodic task. For other variables, last empty is the slot number of the last empty slot; n and ls max are the number of released instances and the starting time of the last instance of τ max , respectively. dl[m] and S[n] are the arrays saving past slots associated deadlines and released instances's starting time. Then, three temporary deadlines (vd k , vd k , vd k ) defined in Section III-B are calculated corresponding to the previous deadline, last empty slot, and last starting time of τ max . When advancing to the past, max dl holds the maximum associated deadline of traced S[n] elements. Under the mentioned condition of limits of how long the release time can be advanced, the expected virtual deadline vd k cannot be earlier than vd k , vd k , vd k , and max dl.

At the beginning of advancing, vd k is initialized to the deadline using the original TBS's formula at line 2. Then three temporary deadlines are calculated from line 4 to line 16. The temporary deadlines corresponding to the previous deadline and last empty slot are computed outside the loop at line 5 and line 12. When the virtual deadline is earlier than or equal to vd k , the virtual deadline is set to vd k , and the algorithm finishes. Then, as mentioned above, the ls max -th slot is one of the checking bound and the corresponding deadline, vd k , is calculated at line 16. Combining these temporary deadlines, a variable bound at line 17 presents the check-bounding deadline of the algorithm. Next, to satisfy the limit of previously-used maximum deadline, for each of the traced S[n] elements, the corresponding vd k is compared to max dl from line 18 to line 33. The virtual deadline obtained after the loop execution satisfies conditions of bound and max dl and therefore it is the expected deadline.

div.head: E. Enhanced points of the algorithm
div.p: In Section III-A, main sources of considerable runtime overhead in the original algorithm are repeated checking of limits. Therefore, enhanced points of the proposed algorithm are aimed to decrease these sources.

The first improved point in the new algorithm is the way to deal with the previous task's deadline and the empty slot. As shown in the Algorithm 1, the two sources are eliminated by moving them out of the loop. This helps to reduce the influence of repeated checking.

The second enhanced point is introduction of checkbounding slot or the last starting time ls max of the task having the maximum period. In the original algorithm, the advancing theoretically recurs backward to the past without any limitations. However, checking slots before ls max is actually unmeaning since the associated deadline of ls max -th slot is always greater than or equal to those of past slots under EDF-based scheduling. The definition of ls max -th slot helps to determine how long past the advancing is performed. The worst (or longest) case of advancing is 2(T max -C max ) + 1 where T max and C max are the period and computation time of τ max , respectively.

The last main point of the algorithm is that checking is done for representative slots. In the original algorithm, to achieve the last limit of previously-used maximum deadline, used slots have to be involved one by one. Therefore, the associated deadlines of all of used slots have to be recorded by array dl[m] sized by m. In a different way, the new algorithm uses only the first slots of instances recorded by array S[n] sized by n. Naturally, n (the numer of released instances) is smaller than m (the number of past slots) unless all of instances are executed in exactly one slot. Using S[n], instead of dl[m], has two advantages. Firstly, the number of times that array S[n] is checked is significantly less than that on array dl [m]. It means that the runtime overheads caused by the loop execution are lowered. Secondly, since array S[n] is smaller, the time and space costs of saving it are more efficient.

div.head: IV. EVALUATION
div.p: The evaluation is done for four requirements: runtime overhead, response time, schedulability, and implementation complexity. Among them, runtime overhead is obviously the targeted one. The software simulation environment based on the instruction set of the Cortex-A9 processor [6][7] is installed. The additional runtime overhead is estimated according to the number of cycles of instructions' execution. Arithmetic, logical, and control operations in the algorithm are involved in the runtime overhead calculation. Simulations are done for the EVRA algorithm together with the original TBS, the original VRA, the improved TBS [8] [9], and the Constant Bandwidth Server (CBS) [10] for the purpose of effectiveness comparison.

1) Runtime overhead: The additional execution runtime overheads are estimated from the information obtained in the simulations. It is assumed that a processor's clock frequency is 100MHz and the tick length is 0.1ms. The simulation environment is built according to the TBS server and preemptive EDF algorithm similarly to that in [2]. Each task set in simulations consists of both periodic and aperiodic tasks. The processor utilization of the periodic tasks (U p ) is from 60% to 95%. The utilization interval is of 5%. Meanwhile, the utilization of the aperiodic tasks is about 2% in the observation period (100,000 ticks). All the aperiodic servers are supposed to have the utilization U s = 1 -U p .

Figure 6 shows simulation results of the maximum runtime overhead per tick in comparison with the original TBS and the original VRA. TBS+EVRA denotes the runtime overhead of the EVRA algorithm. TBS and TBS+VRA are the results of the original TBS and original VRA algorithms, respectively. As shown, the maximum runtime overhead of the EVRA is lower than that of TBS+VRA and greater than original TBS. At U p = 95%, the maximum total runtime overhead/tick of the EVRA is around 327 whereas that of TBS+VRA is around 747. The EVRA is effective to reduce approximately 56% of the runtime overhead compared to TBS+VRA. This improved result allows to apply this technique to actual real time system. In addition, the maximum runtime overhead is also compared with that of the improved TBS and CBS algorithms in Figure 7. TB* and CBS show the results of the runtime overhead of the improved TBS and CBS algorithm, respectively. The EVRA algorithm, together with the original VRA, has a very lower additional overhead compared with the improved TBS although it still has a higher overhead compared with the CBS algorithm. As shown in simulation results, the additional overhead of the CBS algorithm seems equivalent to that of the original TBS. 2) Response time: Along with evaluating the runtime overhead, there is another considerable requirement, that is, response time. The EVRA algorithm is proposed with an expectation of keeping the same responsiveness with that of the original VRA algorithm. Results of response time are therefore shown in Figure 8. The response time for EVRA is equal to VRA and clearly better than original TBS. Although it can improve the responsiveness of the original TBS, the EVRA algorithm still generates longer response times than the improved TBS and CBS algorithms. Overall, the responsiveness of the improved TBS is the best. However, it can be expected that combination of VRA/EVRA and adaptive TBS [1] (instead of TBS) would exhibit shorter response times than CBS.

div.head: V. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper, an enhanced virtual release advancing algorithm is proposed. This is an enhancement of virtual release advancing in terms of runtime overhead. The runtime overhead is significantly reduced while the schedulability and responsiveness are guaranteed. With lower runtime overhead, the new technique is more applicable to precise real-time systems. In addition, this technique reduces the implementation complexity of the previous algorithm by determining the bound of advancing. In the future, the proposed algorithm will be evaluated in combination with the adaptive TBS technique [1]. In addition, hardware implementation of the proposed algorithm is considered to further reduce the runtime overhead.
